transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah… thanks. I’m here because I keep finding myself getting up when I’m supposed to just stay put. Like during client interviews, or when I’m tutoring someone, even at book club—which is funny because you’d think book club would be relaxed, but apparently wandering into the kitchen while someone’s talking about chapter six is “distracting.” 

It’s not that I’m trying to be rude. I just… I can’t seem to sit and listen for very long, and people are starting to notice.
When you're not sitting still, do you also find yourself feeling especially restless, fidgety, or like you have to act on impulses without thinking?

Yeah, definitely fidgety. Like if I’m at the computer going through records—which is a huge part of my work, just endless databases and old filings—my foot is bouncing the whole time under the desk, or I’m clicking a pen without realizing it.

And then I’ll be shifting around in the chair so much that I actually lose my place in what I’m reading. Which is ridiculous, because I’m supposed to be finding details, not… you know, conducting a percussion section with office supplies.
Did you have similar issues with restlessness or being unable to sit still when you were a child, or is this something that started more recently?

Oh, no, this goes way back. My grade-school report cards always had some version of, “She’s bright, but she can’t stay in her seat,” or “needs to wait her turn.” My mother still jokes that I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through—which, I mean, considering what I ended up doing for work, is maybe a little too on the nose.

But yes, it wasn’t just recent. It was there when I was a kid.
When you're trying to focus on tasks, like when you're working with databases or listening in meetings, do you find it hard to stay focused or get easily distracted by things around you?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I do lose my place sometimes, but I can’t tell if that’s because I’m distracted by things around me or because I’m just… moving around too much in my own chair, if that makes sense.

In meetings, I try to listen, and then someone’s coffee cup is squeaking or there’s a siren outside—actually, living near a busy street will teach you a lot about how many different kinds of sirens there are—but I don’t know if that’s unusual or just normal noticing things. So… I’m not sure I’d say it’s the main issue. The sitting still part is the thing I notice more.
Do you find it hard to stay focused on tasks, even when there aren’t obvious distractions around you, like your mind wandering or losing track of what you're supposed to be doing?

I’m not sure how to separate that out, honestly. If there’s nothing obvious going on around me, I can usually tell myself, “Okay, just finish this one thing,” but then I’ll realize I’ve been staring at the same line for a while.

But I don’t know if that’s my mind wandering exactly, or if I’m just tired of sitting there. I’m terrible at answering these cleanly, sorry. It’s like when you’re watching surveillance footage and after twenty minutes every gray sedan starts to look important, and then you start thinking about whether you locked your own car, and—sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

So… maybe sometimes? But I haven’t really noticed it as the big problem the way I notice the restlessness.

Do you experience this restlessness or need to move around in different settings, like at home when you're trying to relax, or only in situations where you feel you 'should' be still, like work or meetings?

It’s definitely not only work or meetings. I mean, those make it more obvious because everyone’s sitting there like normal adults and I’m shifting around like I’m waiting for a wiretap to come through.

But even at home, on days when I don’t have field work, I don’t really… stop. I’ll start unpacking boxes, then suddenly I’m reorganizing case files, then I’m running errands like I’m chasing a lead somewhere. And half the time there isn’t even anything urgent. I just have a hard time being off duty, I guess.

My sister can sit on a couch and watch a whole movie, and I’ll be up halfway through checking the mail or moving something from one room to another. So yes, it follows me home.
Would you say that this restlessness or need to keep moving happens almost every day, or does it come and go depending on your mood or situation?

Almost every day, I think. It’s not really tied to being in a bad mood or anything.

Like, even on days when I don’t have field work, I still end up moving from one thing to another—unpacking boxes, then reorganizing case files, then suddenly I’m out running errands like I’m chasing down a lead, except there isn’t actually a lead. It’s just me not knowing how to… be off duty, I guess.

So yes, it comes up a lot. It’s pretty constant.
Do you ever find yourself acting on impulse without thinking, like interrupting others, blurting out answers, or making sudden decisions without considering the consequences?

Yes… that one, yes. I don’t always notice it in the moment, which is probably part of the problem.

If I hear the junior detectives talking through a lead, I’ll just sort of jump in—questions, advice, “Did you check this?”—before anyone asked me. And then two minutes later I realize I wasn’t actually part of that conversation. Same thing in my building sometimes, if a neighbor’s talking in the hallway and I catch one piece of it, I’ll stick my head out and comment like I’ve been invited.

It’s not usually meant to be rude. It feels like the thought gets ahead of me, and then afterward I think, okay, you barged into that.
Do you often have trouble finishing tasks, lose your train of thought easily, or find that your mind wanders a lot even when you're trying to focus?

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean… everyone loses their train of thought sometimes, right?

With my work, I usually can follow something if it’s important enough—like if there’s a case file in front of me, or someone’s story has a detail that doesn’t line up. Then I can latch onto it. But finishing regular things… I don’t know. Sometimes I’ll start one thing and then another thing is suddenly more pressing, or it feels more pressing, and then I’m in a different room wondering why I went in there.

Sorry, that’s probably not what you asked. My mind does wander, but I don’t know if it’s more than normal. Like, if I’m trying to read something dry, forget it, but if it’s a witness statement I can usually stay with it. Mostly.

Do you find it difficult to stay focused on tasks even when you're not feeling restless or needing to move around, such as when you're reading something interesting or working on a task you care about?

I’m not sure. I mean, if it’s something I care about, I can sometimes stay with it pretty well.

Like, there was this old property record I was looking at last month—not exciting to most people, probably, but it had this odd transfer history, and I remember sitting there longer than I meant to because I wanted to figure out why the names kept changing. Then I realized I’d skipped lunch, which sounds like focus, I guess.

But if you mean, do I drift off even when I’m interested… maybe sometimes? It’s hard to separate from everything else. If I’m not restless, I don’t always notice what my mind is doing until I’ve already gone sideways. Does that make sense?

Can you think of a time when you were in a situation that required you to stay quiet, remain seated, or wait your turn—like in a meeting, a waiting room, or even a movie theater—where you felt like you just couldn’t do it and ended up acting impulsively or leaving early?

Yes. That’s actually one of the things that made me think, okay, maybe I should talk to someone.

I’ll be in a client interview, and I know I’m supposed to sit there and just let them talk—people tell you more if you don’t crowd them, I know that. But I’ll get up to “just grab” a file, or check the window, or refill coffee, and then I’m pacing behind the chair while they’re still answering me. It’s embarrassing because I can feel them noticing.

It happens other places too. I tutor sometimes, and I’ll tell the kid, “Okay, you work through that problem,” and then I’m up straightening books or moving around the table instead of just staying put. Book club is worse, honestly—everyone’s sitting politely discussing chapter six, and I’m up getting water, looking at the shelves, coming back, leaving again. Not because I hate the book. Well, sometimes the book is terrible, but that’s not really the point.

The point is, yes—I have trouble just sitting and listening when that’s what the situation calls for.
Can you think of times when you were trying to focus on something important, but your mind just wouldn’t stay on track, even if you weren’t restless or distracted by things around you?

I’m not sure I can think of a clean example of that. If my mind goes off track, I usually assume it’s because something else pulled at me, or because I got up and started doing something else, or because the thing wasn’t holding me.

I mean… “important” is tricky. Sometimes important things are boring, which feels unfair, but there it is. Like forms. Forms are important, but they’re designed by people who apparently want everyone to suffer. Sorry—that’s not really the question.

If I’m sitting still and there’s nothing around distracting me, and it’s something I actually care about… I don’t know that I notice my mind refusing to stay put. Maybe it happens, but I don’t have a specific time popping into my head. Usually there’s some reason I can point to, or at least I think there is.

Can you think of a time when you were trying to focus on something that wasn’t boring or uninteresting to you—something you actually cared about—where your mind still wandered or you had trouble keeping your thoughts organized, even though you weren’t restless or distracted by anything around you?

I’m trying to think of one, and I keep circling back to… not really? Or not one that feels clean enough to say, “Yes, that happened.”

If it’s something I actually care about, I can usually stay with it, sometimes too much, honestly. Like I’ll follow one little thread because it seems important, and then—well, that’s not exactly mind wandering, that’s more me chasing the thread. Which, in my line of work, can be useful or it can be a complete waste of two hours depending on whether the thread turns out to be anything.

But if you mean I’m sitting quietly, not fidgeting, no phone buzzing, no person interrupting me, and I’m interested in the thing… I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed my thoughts scattering in that situation. It’s hard for me to separate “my mind wandered” from “I found another angle and went after that.” Does that answer it?
Can you think of times when you were in a completely relaxed setting, with no pressure to be still or focused, where you still felt an inner sense of restlessness or an urge to move around?

Yes—actually, maybe more when there’s no pressure, because then there’s nothing forcing me into one lane.

Like on days when I don’t have field work, I’ll think, great, I can relax, have a normal quiet day. And then somehow I’m unpacking a box I’ve ignored for six months, then halfway through that I’m reorganizing case files, then I remember an errand and I’m out the door like I’m chasing a lead. Which is ridiculous, because nobody is paying me to investigate whether I’m out of paper towels.

It’s not even that I feel stressed exactly. It’s more like being off duty doesn’t really click on. I have a hard time just… being home and doing nothing. I keep finding some reason to move around or start something.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem, or feeling like you can’t control your anxiety about different parts of your life?

I don’t know that I’d call it worrying a lot. I mean, I worry when there’s something to worry about—bills, a client acting strange, my car making a noise that definitely wasn’t there yesterday. Although with cars I always think I’ll remember the sound later and describe it to the mechanic, and then of course I sound like I’m doing bird calls in a garage.

But anxiety that I can’t control, across everything? I’m not sure. I don’t really sit around feeling anxious for no reason, at least not that I notice. If anything, I usually try to figure out what the problem is and do something about it. Sometimes there isn’t a problem, and then I just… move on, I guess. So, no, not in the way you’re describing, I don’t think.

Sorry, that’s probably not what you asked. My mind does wander, but I don’t know if it’s more than normal. Like, if I’m trying to read something dry, forget it, but if it’s a witness statement I can usually stay with it. Mostly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of inattention that are independent of restlessness, which would support F90.0 (ADHD) over F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder).
doctor.question: Do you find it difficult to stay focused on tasks even when you're not feeling restless or needing to move around, such as when you're reading something interesting or working on a task you care about?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty sustaining attention or focus independent of restlessness, including during interesting or meaningful tasks. The provided symptom profile does not include a specific inattention/focus symptom that matches this directly.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean, if it’s something I care about, I can sometimes stay with it pretty well.

Like, there was this old property record I was looking at last month—not exciting to most people, probably, but it had this odd transfer history, and I remember sitting there longer than I meant to because I wanted to figure out why the names kept changing. Then I realized I’d skipped lunch, which sounds like focus, I guess.

But if you mean, do I drift off even when I’m interested… maybe sometimes? It’s hard to separate from everything else. If I’m not restless, I don’t always notice what my mind is doing until I’ve already gone sideways. Does that make sense?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of hyperactivity or impulsivity in multiple settings, which would support the diagnosis of ADHD (F90.0) over generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1).
doctor.question: Can you think of a time when you were in a situation that required you to stay quiet, remain seated, or wait your turn—like in a meeting, a waiting room, or even a movie theater—where you felt like you just couldn’t do it and ended up acting impulsively or leaving early?

target_item.name: Leaving_Seat
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put—during client interviews, tutoring sessions, even book club—and people are starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen.
target_item.reason: The question most directly asks about situations where remaining seated is expected and the patient feels unable to do so, possibly leaving early.

patient.answer:
Yes. That’s actually one of the things that made me think, okay, maybe I should talk to someone.

I’ll be in a client interview, and I know I’m supposed to sit there and just let them talk—people tell you more if you don’t crowd them, I know that. But I’ll get up to “just grab” a file, or check the window, or refill coffee, and then I’m pacing behind the chair while they’re still answering me. It’s embarrassing because I can feel them noticing.

It happens other places too. I tutor sometimes, and I’ll tell the kid, “Okay, you work through that problem,” and then I’m up straightening books or moving around the table instead of just staying put. Book club is worse, honestly—everyone’s sitting politely discussing chapter six, and I’m up getting water, looking at the shelves, coming back, leaving again. Not because I hate the book. Well, sometimes the book is terrible, but that’s not really the point.

The point is, yes—I have trouble just sitting and listening when that’s what the situation calls for.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of inattention that are not better explained by restlessness or external distractions, which would help differentiate between ADHD (F90.0) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1).
doctor.question: Can you think of times when you were trying to focus on something important, but your mind just wouldn’t stay on track, even if you weren’t restless or distracted by things around you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty sustaining attention or mind-wandering even without restlessness or external distraction, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can think of a clean example of that. If my mind goes off track, I usually assume it’s because something else pulled at me, or because I got up and started doing something else, or because the thing wasn’t holding me.

I mean… “important” is tricky. Sometimes important things are boring, which feels unfair, but there it is. Like forms. Forms are important, but they’re designed by people who apparently want everyone to suffer. Sorry—that’s not really the question.

If I’m sitting still and there’s nothing around distracting me, and it’s something I actually care about… I don’t know that I notice my mind refusing to stay put. Maybe it happens, but I don’t have a specific time popping into my head. Usually there’s some reason I can point to, or at least I think there is.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of inattention independently from restlessness, which would support a diagnosis of ADHD (F90.0) over generalized anxiety (F41.1).
doctor.question: Can you think of a time when you were trying to focus on something that wasn’t boring or uninteresting to you—something you actually cared about—where your mind still wandered or you had trouble keeping your thoughts organized, even though you weren’t restless or distracted by anything around you?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about inattention or mind-wandering during interesting tasks without restlessness or external distraction, but the provided symptom profile only covers hyperactive/impulsive symptoms and related impairment/onset/duration.

patient.answer:
I’m trying to think of one, and I keep circling back to… not really? Or not one that feels clean enough to say, “Yes, that happened.”

If it’s something I actually care about, I can usually stay with it, sometimes too much, honestly. Like I’ll follow one little thread because it seems important, and then—well, that’s not exactly mind wandering, that’s more me chasing the thread. Which, in my line of work, can be useful or it can be a complete waste of two hours depending on whether the thread turns out to be anything.

But if you mean I’m sitting quietly, not fidgeting, no phone buzzing, no person interrupting me, and I’m interested in the thing… I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed my thoughts scattering in that situation. It’s hard for me to separate “my mind wandered” from “I found another angle and went after that.” Does that answer it?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of hyperactivity or restlessness in settings where there is no expectation to be still, to assess if this is a pervasive issue consistent with ADHD.
doctor.question: Can you think of times when you were in a completely relaxed setting, with no pressure to be still or focused, where you still felt an inner sense of restlessness or an urge to move around?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: On days when I don't have field work, I still move from unpacking boxes to reorganizing case files to running errands like I'm chasing a lead, and I have a hard time just being off duty.
target_item.reason: The question asks about inner restlessness or an urge to move around even in relaxed settings, which most directly matches being constantly active or 'driven by a motor.'

patient.answer:
Yes—actually, maybe more when there’s no pressure, because then there’s nothing forcing me into one lane.

Like on days when I don’t have field work, I’ll think, great, I can relax, have a normal quiet day. And then somehow I’m unpacking a box I’ve ignored for six months, then halfway through that I’m reorganizing case files, then I remember an errand and I’m out the door like I’m chasing a lead. Which is ridiculous, because nobody is paying me to investigate whether I’m out of paper towels.

It’s not even that I feel stressed exactly. It’s more like being off duty doesn’t really click on. I have a hard time just… being home and doing nothing. I keep finding some reason to move around or start something.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of worry or anxiety that are excessive, difficult to control, and present more days than not, which would support generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) over ADHD (F90.0).
doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem, or feeling like you can’t control your anxiety about different parts of your life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worry or uncontrollable anxiety, which is not covered by the provided ADHD hyperactive/impulsive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d call it worrying a lot. I mean, I worry when there’s something to worry about—bills, a client acting strange, my car making a noise that definitely wasn’t there yesterday. Although with cars I always think I’ll remember the sound later and describe it to the mechanic, and then of course I sound like I’m doing bird calls in a garage.

But anxiety that I can’t control, across everything? I’m not sure. I don’t really sit around feeling anxious for no reason, at least not that I notice. If anything, I usually try to figure out what the problem is and do something about it. Sometimes there isn’t a problem, and then I just… move on, I guess. So, no, not in the way you’re describing, I don’t think.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of persistent restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, impulsivity, and lifelong pattern are consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation (F90.0). Generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) was considered due to the patient's ability to focus on tasks of interest and absence of excessive worry or uncontrollable anxiety despite significant restlessness. This turn further ruled out primary anxiety as the main disorder.
